claims.claimText: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

claims.claimText: Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.
claims.claimValue: University of Toronto graduate students must clearly describe and cite any generative AI tools used in thesis research or writing.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Careful attention must be paid in the thesis to appropriately citing and describing any use of generative AI tools in the research process. It must be clear to the reader which generative AI tools were used, as well as how and why they were used.

claims.claimText: The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Undergraduate and graduate students may use GenAI tools as learning aids, for example, to summarize information or test their understanding of a topic. These tools should be used in a manner similar to consulting library books, online sources, peers, or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has stated that AI tools are not otherwise permitted in the course. These uses typically do not need to be cited or disclosed.

claims.claimText: Unless they have explicit permission from the instructor, University of Toronto students may not upload, copy, input or share course materials created or provided by the instructor, teaching assistants or the University (such as lecture slides, recordings, test questions, solutions and rubrics) to a generative AI tool that the University has not approved for that purpose.
